title: x/build: add LUCI openbsd-ppc64 builder
body: I'm following the Dashboard builders instructions to add hostname openbsd-ppc64-reporter. I attached the CSR after renaming it because GitHub would not allow the requested openbsd-ppc64-reporter.csr filename.

symptoms_visible: I am setting up openbsd-ppc64-reporter as a new Go LUCI builder and have submitted its CSR.
N0.label: N0 builder enrollment requested

symptoms_visible: Using the issued certificate, I get a plausible-looking luci_machine_tokend/token.json.
N1.label: N1 certificate and builder definition ready

symptoms_visible: bootstrapswarm reads my token file and starts the swarming bot, but the handshake returns HTTP 403 Forbidden.
N2.label: N2 initial swarming handshake rejected

symptoms_visible: The same bootstrapswarm invocation now connects without the earlier 403, but assigned work fails because an openbsd-ppc64 CIPD package cannot be resolved.
N3.label: N3 transient authentication error cleared

symptoms_visible: After rebuilding bootstrapswarm from latest, it exits because -token-file-path is no longer a defined flag.
N4.label: N4 updated bootstrap command rejects obsolete flag

symptoms_visible: After dropping -token-file-path and keeping LUCI_MACHINE_TOKEN set, bootstrapswarm starts normally, but the build fails to resolve golang/bootstrap-go/openbsd-ppc64@1.21.0.
N5.label: N5 bot starts but bootstrap package is absent

symptoms_visible: With the bootstrap package available, the LUCI build reaches passing runtime tests, but later reports resource failures and the OpenBSD machine can panic under the builder workload.
The machine still has about 23 GB free, so it is not simply out of physical RAM.
N6.label: N6 builds execute but expose resource and kernel limits

symptoms_visible: After raising the swarming login class datasize limit to 8 GB and rebooting, the machine still eventually panics with a kernel allocation failure.
N6_x.label: N6_x larger data limit aftermath

symptoms_visible: The openbsd-ppc64 machine receives and completes LUCI work reliably enough for the migration, and I have stopped the old coordinator buildlet.
Occasional high-load kernel lock failures remain an OpenBSD problem that I can reproduce without Go, rather than a LUCI onboarding failure.
N_terminal.label: terminal LUCI migration complete

question_patterns: Can you install the resulting certificate and confirm whether luci_machine_tokend creates a token.json file?
After using the issued certificate, what does the token setup produce?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Using the certificate, I get a plausible-looking luci_machine_tokend/token.json.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The certificate is rejected and luci_machine_tokend does not create token.json.
The token file is created at a different path, but it otherwise looks valid.

solution.intent: Issue the machine certificate and define the requested openbsd-ppc64 builder in the LUCI configuration so onboarding can continue.
solution.concrete_example: Sign the submitted CSR, return the certificate, and add the openbsd-ppc64 builder definition to the LUCI configuration.

edges.comment: The maintainer returned a signed certificate and submitted the LUCI builder definition; the reporter confirmed only the observable token-file result.

solution.intent: Proceed with the documented machine-side setup and start bootstrapswarm using the generated machine token.
solution.concrete_example: Continue with the next Dashboard builders steps and start bootstrapswarm with the token produced by luci_machine_tokend.

edges.comment: Continuing the documented setup persistently installs and starts the swarming machinery. The resulting 403 and token-path details were later volunteered by the reporter.

question_patterns: Does the handshake failure persist if you retry the same invocation later?
Please restart the bot and report whether the HTTP error is still present.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I retried the same bootstrapswarm invocation and no longer get the 403. I tried it several more times over the following week without seeing that error again.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every restart still returns HTTP 403, and the bot never completes a handshake.
One retry still failed, but subsequent retries connected using the same token file.

question_patterns: After the bot reconnects and receives work, what is the first task error shown in its output?
Can you restart the bot and paste the raw failure from the assigned task?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: After it received work, the task printed: 'Could not resolve version infra/tools/cipd/openbsd-ppc64:git_revision:ec494f363fdfd8cdd5926baad4508d562b7353d4: no such package: infra/tools/cipd/openbsd-ppc64'.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The task resolves every package successfully and instead fails while compiling the Go runtime.

edges.comment: The retry is a measurement: the reporter supplied the transient outcome and raw package-resolution error. Diagnosing missing server-side platform packaging is engineer-side.

question_patterns: Can you rebuild bootstrapswarm from latest, restart it, and paste any startup error?
Please try the current bootstrapswarm and tell us exactly what it prints.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I rebuilt golang.org/x/build/cmd/bootstrapswarm@latest and tried to restart it, but got an error saying flag -token-file-path was provided but not defined.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The latest bootstrapswarm accepts the command unchanged and starts without an error.

solution.intent: Add server-side package-building support for the new openbsd/ppc64 platform so LUCI tasks can resolve their required tools.
solution.concrete_example: Configure the CIPD package pipeline to produce the required tools for openbsd/ppc64, using a Go toolchain new enough to support that port.
solution.inference_hint: The raw task output says only that the package does not exist. Concluding that the CIPD build pipeline lacks openbsd/ppc64 platform support is the maintainer's diagnosis.

edges.comment: The server-side package work progressed while the reporter later rebuilt the client. The current client exposed a separate command-line compatibility change.

question_patterns: After correcting the startup command, can you restart the bot and paste the next build failure?
Once bootstrapswarm starts, what raw error does the newest assigned build report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It restarted without startup errors. The assigned build then failed with: 'failed to resolve golang/bootstrap-go/openbsd-ppc64@1.21.0: no such package: golang/bootstrap-go/openbsd-ppc64'.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The bot starts and the build resolves the bootstrap package successfully, then fails only in a Go test.
The same missing-package message appears with a different task identifier.

solution.intent: Use LUCI_MACHINE_TOKEN as the supported token-file path configuration and remove the obsolete bootstrapswarm command-line flag.
solution.concrete_example: Keep LUCI_MACHINE_TOKEN set to the token.json path and restart bootstrapswarm without -token-file-path, since the flag was removed in favor of the environment variable.

edges.comment: The reporter removed the obsolete flag, retained the environment variable, and confirmed the bot restarted. The subsequent missing-bootstrap line is raw verification output.

solution.intent: Publish and select a Go 1.22 bootstrap package for openbsd/ppc64, because the requested Go 1.21 bootstrap predates support for the new port.
solution.concrete_example: Create golang/bootstrap-go/openbsd-ppc64 from Go 1.22 and configure this builder to use it instead of requesting the nonexistent 1.21.0 package.
solution.inference_hint: The task output identifies a nonexistent 1.21.0 bootstrap package. Knowing that Go 1.21 cannot build the new openbsd/ppc64 port, and therefore that its bootstrap must be produced with Go 1.22, is maintainer inference.

edges.comment: Once the correct bootstrap became available, builds progressed through compilation and runtime tests, exposing separate machine-resource and OpenBSD kernel issues.

solution.intent: Treat the post-test failure as a simple per-process memory ceiling and raise the swarming account's data-size limit to 8 GB.
solution.concrete_example: Set datasize-max=8192M for the swarming login class, reboot, and rerun the worker.

edges.comment: This was actually tried. Raising the data-size limit did not prevent the machine from panicking, so it is a known blind path rather than the resolution.

question_patterns: Please let the worker run under normal load for a while and report whether it completes useful work reliably enough to retire the old builder.
After the latest configuration changes, can you verify the machine's behavior over multiple builds before we call the migration complete?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The machine is getting substantial LUCI work done and is stable enough for the migration. I now regard the LUCI migration as complete and am no longer running the old buildlet. I still reboot when the separate kernel lock issue appears.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The worker still cannot complete builds and goes offline on every run, so I have kept the old buildlet active.
The worker completes useful builds but needs an occasional reboot during unusually high load.

solution.intent: Finish the migration by tuning the builder for realistic OpenBSD resource and performance limits, while treating the independently reproducible kernel panic as an OS issue rather than a LUCI packaging failure.
solution.concrete_example: Use a swarming login class with maxproc-max=512 and maxproc-cur=256, give the openbsd-ppc64 builder a timeout scale of 3, avoid running the old buildlet in parallel, and continue the independently reproducible high-load kernel-lock investigation in OpenBSD.
solution.inference_hint: The accepted resolution separates two layers: LUCI needed openbsd/ppc64 package and bootstrap support plus realistic timeout/process settings, while the remaining panic was reproduced without Go and belongs to OpenBSD's high-load kernel locking behavior. The final stability report is terminal-side verification and is not required evidence for proposing these changes.

edges.comment: The reporter later recorded that maxproc-max=512 and maxproc-cur=256 sufficed, reproduced the panic without Go, resumed swarming, stopped the old buildlet, and accepted the migration as complete. The maintainer applied timeout scaling and closed after observing sustained useful builds.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the main LUCI onboarding blockers as missing server-side openbsd/ppc64 CIPD and bootstrap artifacts, including the need for a Go 1.22 bootstrap because Go 1.21 does not support the new port.
Must account for the client-side invocation change: current bootstrapswarm uses LUCI_MACHINE_TOKEN and no longer accepts -token-file-path.
Must ground the diagnosis in the collected raw failures: the missing CIPD package, the missing golang/bootstrap-go/openbsd-ppc64@1.21.0 package, and the later resource-related build behavior.
Must not treat the transient HTTP 403, 401, 429, or 500 responses as the final root cause; retries and later successful work showed those errors were temporary.
Must not claim that raising the data-size limit to 8 GB resolves the crashes; the machine still panicked after that change.
Must distinguish the remaining high-load OpenBSD kernel lock problem, which was reproduced without Go, from the completed LUCI migration.

Must tune process and timeout limits, keep machine load reasonable, and have the reporter verify useful work over multiple LUCI builds before declaring the migration complete and retiring the old buildlet.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical systems operator familiar with OpenBSD, source builds, login classes, process limits, certificates, service supervision, and kernel debugging, but new to Go's LUCI builder infrastructure and its dashboards.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, candid, and cooperative; pastes exact logs and timestamps, challenges unclear instructions, offers remote debugging access, and clearly distinguishes observations from uncertainty.
